What

What Willow Tree Care Involves

Willow tree care is species-specific pruning for Salix trees — most often the weeping willow (Salix babylonica), plus smaller ornamental pussy willows. Because willow wood is structurally weak, the work centers on annual deadwood removal, structural pruning, and clearing hazard limbs before they fail. Every visit starts with a free on-site walk and a written estimate from Roubic before any cutting begins.

The distinction that matters with willows: fast growth does not mean they tolerate heavy cutting. Severe reduction and topping remain inappropriate even on a fast-growing species — they trigger weak suckering regrowth and increased decay. When an aging willow's hazard load outgrows reasonable maintenance, the honest answer is removal-and-replant rather than repeated over-pruning.

Why

Four Reasons Homeowners Call Roubic About Willows

The willow scenarios our crew walks most across NE Ohio residential properties.

Branches Failing in Storms

Weeping willow wood is weak and limbs shed routinely — especially in summer storms when full leaves catch wind.

Roots Into Sewer or Septic

Willow roots are aggressive water-seekers that infiltrate sewer lines, septic tanks, and drainage systems.

Clearance & Deadwood

Low, sweeping limbs over roofs, drives, and lawns need annual deadwood removal and structural pruning.

Aging Willow Decision

Many older willows reach a point where hazard load exceeds maintenance — removal-and-replant is the right call.

Common Willow Questions

Willow Tree Care FAQ

Five things NE Ohio homeowners want to know before booking willow work.

Why are branches falling off my weeping willow?
Willow wood is structurally weak, so branch failures are normal — especially in summer storms when full leaves catch wind. Annual deadwood removal and structural pruning reduces the risk. Older willows may have reached a point where the hazard load outgrows maintenance and removal-and-replant is the appropriate outcome.
Can willow roots damage my sewer line?
Yes. Willow roots are aggressive water-seekers and routinely infiltrate sewer lines and septic systems. We recommend planting willows at least 50 ft from any underground utility or septic system. If you have an existing willow near a sewer line, expect ongoing root-intrusion issues.
Should I top my willow?
No — topping is malpractice on any species. Even fast-growing willows respond poorly, producing weak suckering regrowth and increased decay. If clearance is the real issue, correct reduction pruning or removal-and-replant is the right answer, not topping.
How much does willow maintenance cost?
Willow maintenance pruning typically runs $300–$900 per tree depending on size and access. Storm hazard mitigation and removal-and-replant are quoted on-site; removal pricing follows standard tree-removal benchmarks in our Tree Service Cost Guide.
When is the best time to prune a willow?
Structural pruning is best in the dormant season, with deadwood removal handled any time it's needed for safety. Avoid heavy reduction cuts — willows don't respond well to them. A light, consistent annual approach keeps a willow safer than occasional aggressive cutting.
